note: "Prevalence you gave me is 1.5%, so 260 million × 1.5% = 3.9 million people with Corlan's disease" — the case says 1.6%. `misquoteFlat` was on and the misquote check logged `found: []`: `operandLater` dropped the quote because the candidate uses the figure as an operand in a later clause, a guard built for the candidate's OWN derived figures (Marisol b18 t9, "COGS today is 66.7, so … 66.7 minus 14.4"). Here the figure is attributed — "you gave me" — so the later operand is the misquote propagating, not evidence the figure is his. Fixed by `misquoteAttribution`. Rule 6 option 4 asks for one flat sentence; `misquoteSameTurn` says it on this turn, because code's own correction otherwise waits for the checker's verdict a turn later and by t8 he had already fixed it himself.

"You said Nimbrel's net price is about $9,400 per patient per year" — the line says $9,000, and he built $391M of peak sales on it. Correction to the grading: the detector did NOT miss this one. `misquote` at t10 logged `found: [{items:[nimbrel], cited:"is about $9,400"}]`, and the gate released it at t12 ("code's mismatch with nimbrel, and the checker rates \"$9,400\" error/high with no flag (misquoteFlat)"). Nothing flat was ever said because code's correction is owed a turn after the message, and by t12 he had fixed it himself at message 11 ("You gave $9,000, not $9,400"). The spoken line at t10 was the model's Socratic "Which was it, and what does that do to your peak sales number?", which `misquoteFlat` deliberately lets stand. `misquoteSameTurn` says the flat sentence on t10 instead.
